topics.title: Geoemetry is getting complicated
topics.text:
Geometry has always been my weak spot. It just got weirder today. A friend showed me a puzzle that I can't figure out. I know arithmetically what he's describing is clearly wrong but I can't find anything wrong with his geometric logic.



My friend tried to convince me that $8^2=65$

Everyone knows perfectly well that $8 \cdot 8 = 64$, not $65$. But I can't find anything wrong with the logic below:



Assume that there exists an 8 by 8 square. Divide the square such that there exists a 3 by 8 rectangle and a 5 by 8 rectangle. Divide the 3 by 8 rectangle into half diagonally and divide the 5 by 8 into two trapezoids such that the top base is 3 and the bottom base is 5. Potentially, it looks like this:



IMAGE



Rearrange everything so that:



IMAGE



I trust you Aopsers to figure out the rest of the lengths. Point is, I'm pretty sure that $8 \cdot 8 \ne 65$. I can't find fault with the above reasoning. I tried to disprove it by finding the area of the triangles and trapezoids.



My proof that $8^2=64$. The triangles has base 3 height 8, which means $\frac{3 \cdot 8}{2}=12$. The trapezoids have top base 3, bottom base 5, height 5 which gives $\frac{5(3+5)}{2}=20$.$12+12+20+20=64$.

My friend's proof that $8^2=65$. There are two giant triangles with base 5 and height 13 in the rearrangement. $\frac{5 \cdot 13}{2}=32.5$. Therefore, the area is $2 \cdot 32.5=65$.



What am I doing wrong? I know that he's wrong but I can't disprove him. Is there fault somewhere?

topics.title: Explanation why 0! = 1 (credit to my friends)
topics.text:
[quote=My friends]x factorial (written as $x!$) is when you have $x \cdot (x-1) \cdot (x-2) \cdot \cdot \cdot 2 \cdot 1$.  Factorial is also the number of times you can arrange $n$ distinguishable objects in an order.  For example, there are 6 ways to order 3 objects, which also means $3! = 6$.  That can be checked with $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6$.



Now, to answer the question: why does $0! = 1$?



Imagine you have zero objects.  There is only one way to order them - nothing.  So, there is one way to order 0 objects.  Since factorial is the number of ways you can order a number of objects, you get $0! = 1$.

[/quote]

topics.title: A Messy Problem
topics.text:
Your friend is a very bad friend. All your friend wants to do is to is mess up your room. Your room can be rated on a scale from 1 - 10 in messiness, with 10 being very messy and 1 being very clean. It starts off at a 5 rating. A turn is when you clean or your friend makes it messier. Your friend can increase it by 1, but you can decrease it by one. He has a $\frac{1}{4}$ chance of making it cleaner, but you have a $\frac{3}{4}$ of cleaning it up on any given turn. The messiness cannot exceed 10. You can only stop when the messiness rating is 1. What is the expected number of turns you clean up?

topics.title: REUN #3 (5 Question Test)
topics.text:
I have decided to change the format of the upcoming REUN tests by making them 5 questions. Please PM me the answers and solutions before next Wednesday at 4:00 EST.



Rules:

-All radicals and fractions must be in simplest form unless stated otherwise.



-A proof/solution must be provided to earn full points.



-The test will be scored out of 10 points: one and a half points point for each correct answer, and half a point for each valid solution.



*This test is good practice for some harder MATHCOUNTS/AMC10 questions.



Questions1. The We Love Chai Foundation has a number system where letters correspond with numbers depending on their place in the alphabet. For example, the letter $x$ has a value of $24$, because it is the $24$th letter in the alphabet. Words have summed values, which is the corresponding values of the letters added together. For example, the summed value of the word CHAI is $21$, because $3+8+1+9$ is $21.$ How many unique four-letter words have a summed value of $102$ or greater? (ABCD and DCBA are considered unique words.)





2. There is an equation $4x^2+(x+4)^2=y.$ $y$ is a prime positive integer whose digits have a sum of 10. Find the least possible value for $x+y$.





3. A cyclic quadrilateral has a semiperimeter of $7$. If the measures of each side are consecutive positive integers, find the area of this figure. Express answer as a radical in simplest form.





4. Equation $x^2(4+x)=x+6$ has three real solutions. Find the sum of the solutions.





5. The sum $\sum_{x=1}^n x$ is the number of digits in $n+4$-digit positive integer. $\sum_{x=1}^{\frac{1}{10}n} x$ is the number of digits in $n+3$-digit positive integer, $\sum_{x=1}^{\frac{1}{100}n} x$ is the number of digits in $n+2$-digit positive integer, and so on. The digits of $\sum_{x=1}^n x$ are composed of two numbers, and one number appears $4$ times as frequently as the other number. The digits of $\sum_{x=1}^{\frac{1}{10}n} x$ are composed of the same two numbers, and one number appears $3$ times as frequently as the other number, and so on. Find the value of $n$.
